faqs.a: About 1.6 to 1.9 square metres covers most adults, with 1.73 as the classic reference. Children are far lower, often under 1.0.
Chemotherapy and many other drugs are dosed per square metre of BSA because drug clearance tracks body surface better than weight alone. GFR is also reported per 1.73 m2.
faqs.q: Why do doctors use BSA instead of weight?

faqs.a: Du Bois (1916) is the classic and most validated. Mosteller is simpler and within 1-2% of Du Bois for most adults. The differences rarely matter clinically.
faqs.q: Which BSA formula is most accurate?

faqs.a: Yes. Mosteller: BSA = square root of (height in cm x weight in kg / 3600). It is the easiest to compute by hand and is standard in many hospitals.
faqs.q: Is there a simpler BSA formula?

faqs.a: No. BSA formulas are validated for adults and older children. Infant dosing uses dedicated pediatric tables and a clinician's judgment.
faqs.q: Can BSA be used for infants?

faqs.a: This tool estimates BSA correctly, but real dosing also accounts for kidney and liver function, age and the specific drug. Always let a clinician do dosing math.
faqs.q: Can I use this for medicine doses?

body-surface-area-calculator.formula:
Du Bois (1916):
BSA = 0.007184 x weight(kg)^0.425 x height(cm)^0.725
Mosteller (simpler): BSA = sqrt(height(cm) x weight(kg) / 3600).
howTo: Pick metric (cm/kg) or imperial (ft/in, lb) units.
Your body surface area in square metres appears instantly.
Compare it with the typical adult range of about 1.5 to 2.1 m2.
keyFacts: Body surface area (BSA) is the total surface of the human body, measured in square metres.
The Du Bois formula from 1916 remains the most widely used BSA equation in medicine.
A typical adult BSA is about 1.73 m2, which is why kidney function (GFR) is reported per 1.73 m2.
Chemotherapy doses are usually calculated per square metre of BSA.
The simpler Mosteller formula is within 1-2% of Du Bois for most adults.
A 70 kg, 175 cm adult has a BSA of about 1.85 m2.

limitations: An estimate from a 1916 formula based on nine subjects; modern scans differ slightly.
Cannot reflect unusual body shapes or amputations.
Real drug dosing involves more than BSA: kidneys, liver, age and the drug itself.
